n: From here on, Kings dates each ruler by the reign of the king in the other kingdom, weaving the two histories together. Abijam begins to rule Judah in Jeroboam’s eighteenth year (about 913 BC).
Abijam reigns only three years. His mother Maachah was a granddaughter (“daughter” can mean descendant) of Absalom.

f.g: a form of Absalom, David’s son.

n: He repeated his father’s sins. His heart was not whole toward the Lord the way David’s had been.

f.g: whole, undivided in loyalty.

n: Even so, the Lord kept David’s “lamp” burning—preserving his dynasty and Jerusalem because of the promise made to David.
David is held up as the model king, faithful in everything except his grievous sin with Bathsheba and the death of her husband Uriah. Even the ideal king had a serious failing on record.

f.w: the matter of Uriah the Hittite

n: The hostility between the kingdoms that began under Rehoboam continued.

f.g: some manuscripts read ‘Abijam’ here, matching verse 7.

n: Abijam’s deeds are in Judah’s royal records. Chronicles adds a battle where he called on Israel to return to the Lord.

f.w: there was war between Abijam and Jeroboam

n: Abijam dies, and his son Asa becomes king.
Asa begins his reign about 911 BC, in Jeroboam’s twentieth year.
Asa reigns a long forty-one years. “Maachah” here is his grandmother, who kept the title of queen mother.

f.g: ‘mother’ here likely means grandmother, the reigning queen mother.

n: Asa is the first king of Judah after the division to be called righteous like David.
He launches a reform: removing shrine prostitutes and the idols his predecessors had set up.

f.g: cult prostitutes associated with fertility worship.
Hebrew gillulim, a contemptuous word, perhaps ‘dung-idols.’

n: Asa shows courage by removing his own grandmother from her powerful position and burning her Asherah image in the Kidron Valley. Faithfulness to God sometimes requires difficult family choices.

f.g: an ‘obscene image’ for Asherah, the Canaanite mother-goddess.
the valley just east of Jerusalem.

n: The local “high places” remained, likely shrines where people still worshiped the Lord improperly outside the temple. Still, Asa’s heart was loyal to the Lord.

f.g: local hilltop shrines, discouraged once the temple was built.

n: He restored dedicated treasure—silver, gold, and vessels—to the temple, refilling what Shishak had taken.
Asa faced constant conflict with Baasha, the new king of Israel.
Baasha fortified Ramah, just five miles north of Jerusalem, to blockade Judah and stop people from crossing over to the south.

f.g: a town in Benjamin on the main road north of Jerusalem.
allow.

n: Rather than seeking the Lord, Asa empties the temple and palace treasuries to bribe Ben-hadad of Damascus. Chronicles reports that a prophet rebuked him for trusting a foreign king instead of God.

f.g: ‘son of Hadad,’ a title used by several Aramean kings.

n: Asa appeals to an old alliance and asks Ben-hadad to break his treaty with Israel.

f.g: treaty, alliance.

n: Ben-hadad accepts the bribe and attacks Israel’s northern towns around the Sea of Galilee.

f.g: the area around the Sea of Galilee (Chinnereth).
the northern tribal territory west of Galilee.

n: With war on his northern border, Baasha abandons Ramah and pulls back to his capital, Tirzah.
Asa drafts every man in Judah to haul away Baasha’s building materials and uses them to fortify his own border towns of Geba and Mizpah.

f.g: no one was excused from the labor.
‘watchtower,’ a strategic town in Benjamin.

n: Asa’s achievements are recorded in Judah’s records. In old age he suffered a disease in his feet; Chronicles notes he sought physicians rather than the Lord.
Asa dies and his son Jehoshaphat, another righteous king, succeeds him.
The story returns north. Jeroboam’s son Nadab reigns only about two years.
Nadab continues his father’s calf worship.
Baasha, from the tribe of Issachar, assassinates Nadab while the army is besieging the Philistine town of Gibbethon. Israel’s throne becomes a prize seized by force.

f.g: plotted a coup.
a Philistine-controlled town west of Israel’s hill country.

n: Baasha kills Nadab and takes the throne.
Baasha wipes out Jeroboam’s entire family, fulfilling Ahijah’s prophecy. God used Baasha’s violence to accomplish the judgment, though Baasha himself was not righteous.

f.w: according unto the saying of the LORD

n: The cause, again, was the sin of Jeroboam that led all Israel astray.
Nadab’s acts are recorded in Israel’s chronicles.
The note about war between Asa and Baasha repeats verse 16, framing Baasha’s reign.
Baasha rules Israel from Tirzah for twenty-four years.

f.g: Israel’s capital until Omri built Samaria.

n: Though he destroyed Jeroboam’s family for its sin, Baasha commits the same sin himself.

f.w: walked in the way of Jeroboam
